Taiwan-US-China relations: Takeaways from President Tsai's US visit – Monday, April 10th at 10:15 AM New York, 07:15 AM San Francisco, 11:15 AM Brasilia, 03:15 PM UK| Register here
Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen arrived to fanfare in New York on 31 March. After visiting Central America, she will stop for a meeting with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California on 5 April. Third in line to the presidency, McCarthy will be the senior-most US official to meet with a sitting Taiwan president on US soil. Beijing denounced the visit and may employ a show of force and other measures. Join us to discuss the visit's effects on relations between the island, the mainland, and the US.

Eurasia Group’s weekly roundup of top stories
eg update from Ian Bremmer (05.04.23) | Read here
This week, Ian shares the latest on Russia, namely the biggest headline regarding Russia’s arrest of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges. He talks about TikTok and technology being the fastest deteriorating piece of Us-China relations. With the indictment of Trump, the United States has made political history yet again. Finally, Israel hits pause on crisis.
Latin America
Mexico: Treatment of Iberdrola will not extend to other companies in sector (04.05.23) | Read here
On 4 April, power generator Iberdrola announced it will sell most of its Mexican assets to a private investment fund partly owned by Mexico’s National Infrastructure Fund (Fonadin); the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) will become the assets’ new operator. President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador’s administration has consistently targeted the Spanish company with criticism and harsh regulatory treatment; he believes it had received special treatment in the past and had direct connections to his political foes. The president wants to increase CFE’s role in the sector, but he is unlikely to push other companies out and will follow a more nuanced approach toward other investors.
Guatemala: Rios is early presidential favorite as official campaign gets underway (04.05.23) | Read here
Far-right candidate Zury Rios is the early presidential frontrunner ahead of the 25 June first-round presidential election; she will likely face center-left former first lady Sandra Torres in an August runoff, in which Rios would have an advantage owing to Torres’s high rejection rates. The exclusion of antiestablishment candidates Roberto Arzu and Thelma Cabrera from the race will deepen voter discontent and likely increase abstention; center-right Edmond Mulet could emerge as an alternative, but his candidacy is also in question. Rios and Torres represent broad continuity on economic policy and resistance to greater transparency; the latter issue will ensure persistent tensions with the US, though President Joe Biden’s administration will continue to focus on targeted sanctions.
Brazil: Laxer rules for sanitation contracts will affect private investment opportunities (04.05.23) | Read here
At 4 pm (Brazil time) on 5 April, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will sign two decrees reviewing regulations issued by the Jair Bolsonaro administration detailing the 2020 sanitation reform law. The revision will make it easier for state-owned water utilities to keep their current contracts, reducing pressure for privatizations. The administration will not pursue changes to the 2020 legislation, sparing the reform’s main pillars: mandatory tenders for new contracts and the 2033 deadline to universalize coverage. Still, the upcoming specifications will allow state governors who do not want private partners to circumvent compulsory auctions and maintain their SOEs, despite the government’s encouragement of public-private partnerships (PPP). As Eurasia Group expected, the decrees will allow municipalities to hire PPPs with more flexibility by scrapping the 25% outsourcing limit.
Peru: Threats to Boluarte’s position will persist after failed motion to oust her (04.04.23) | Read here
On 4 April, congress rejected an impeachment motion against President Dina Boluarte on the grounds of “permanent moral incapacity,” the first effort to oust Boluarte since she took office in December. But the government will remain extremely fragile and is unlikely to survive until July 2026. Protests have subsided and the attention of authorities recently shifted to responding to rains and flooding in several parts of the country. But public support for Boluarte and congress remains extremely low. The government will remain focused on its survival, and no meaningful reforms are likely to advance. Moreover, public discontent will persist in the long run, particularly if demands for early elections are ignored. Radical and antiestablishment candidates will probably be competitive in a crowded electoral field.
Brazil: Deal on first batch of provisional measures favors Lula’s agenda in congress (04.04.23) | Read here
On 4 April, Institutional Relations Minister Alexandre Padilha announced that the administration struck a deal with both houses of parliament about the procedures to deliberate on the first 13 provisional measures (MPs) enacted by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva since 1 January. The arrangement does not solve the ongoing procedural dispute between Lira and Pacheco over provisional measures but eases the pressure concerning the first bills enacted by the Lula administration—which could expire between late May and early June. The deal clears the way for Lula’s early priorities, and the administration needs to have Lira and Pacheco reach a compromise over MPs procedures.
Brazil: Lessons from new fiscal framework and next steps (04.03.23) | Read here
The new fiscal framework represents a win for the economic team and suggests President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is sensitive to the need to signal fiscal responsibility. The administration will not have much difficulty securing approval of its new fiscal anchor in congress by June or July, but it will achieve only partial success advancing the measures to be unveiled this week to boost revenue by BRL 100 billion-150 billion reais given the competing need to bring the VAT reform to a vote in June. The fiscal rule, along with the likely approval of VAT reform, reinforces the country’s neutral short-term political trajectory; however, difficulties generating sufficient revenue to meet primary surplus targets, along with Lula’s poor reaction function if he loses popular support, are key risk factors to track.
Mexico: Morena’s push to gain control of INE’s board yields mixed results (03.31.23) | Read here
The lower house selected Guadalupe Taddei, who is close to the administration, as the new head of the National Electoral Institute (INE). Morena and the administration were unable to nominate loyalists to all four vacancies, however. The INE’s eleven-member board now has eight Morena-designated commissioners, out of which three have been highly independent and two of the incoming ones are unlikely to bend in favor of the administration. This process will not stop further attacks against the INE, as President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador remains intent on decreasing as much as possible its leeway to monitor campaign spending and electoral violations. Thus, we expect further budget cuts down the line and a weaker board that will struggle to limit Morena’s electoral excesses in 2024.
Mexico: Central bank will remain focused on inflation with no political interference (03.31.23) | Read here
On 30 March, the central bank increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The board of governors is aware of perceptions of its weakness but will remain conservative, believing that it will take some time to achieve its 3% inflation target. President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador has previously publicly questioned rate increases but is primarily concerned about inflation and will continue to respect Banxico’s independence.
Europe
Poland: Opposition loses support, but its current travails may only be temporary (04.06.23) | Read here
Friction within the liberal opposition is causing a loss of support for pro-EU parties, while the “United Right” alliance of the conservative Law and Justice party (PiS) and its junior partner Solidarity Poland has arrested its decline in the polls. That said, this phenomenon might only be temporary; the likely unification of at least two liberal opposition parties in the coming weeks, and the potential nomination of Warsaw Mayor Rafal Trzaskowski as the opposition’s lead candidate instead of former prime minister Donald Tusk, could help the liberal opposition recuperate its lost support. The United Right will also face challenges in the coming weeks; for now, Eurasia Group is maintaining its 65% probability of a pro-EU, liberal opposition government emerging after the elections.
UK: Sunak is back in the race, but is unlikely to catch Labour (04.04.23) | Read here
Having delivered a string of policy wins and restored unity to the Conservative Party, local elections on 4 May are no longer decisive for Prime Minister Rishi Sunak’s government—or his own fate. As such, Eurasia Group is reducing the odds of a Boris Johnson comeback to 10% from 30%. Eurasia Group’s basecase for next year’s general elections—most likely in October 2024—remains a Labour majority (60% odds); we also assign a 30% probability to a hung parliament that results in a Labour minority government with informal support from the Liberal Democrats and/or the Scottish Nationalist Party and a 10% probability to a Tory majority.
Germany, Sustainability: Tackling a phaseout of Russian fossil fuels while accelerating the green transition (04.04.23) | Read here
Germany is attempting to phase out previously high Russian fossil fuel imports while enabling a green transition that continues to supply its heavy industry with reliable, affordable, and clean energy. The timeline for policy action is to first resolve the emergency by replacing all Russian fossil fuels with alternative suppliers (in 2022/2023), then move into a medium-term adaptation process by establishing the regulatory foundations to deploy the technologies needed to cut emissions (2023/2024); afterward, officials will launch the mass deployment of all decarbonized systems to enable clean and affordable energy supply, by 2030. The green energy and industry transition will require substantial energy and industrial government support programs at the national and EU levels, as well as deeper EU cooperation and global supply chain partnerships; it will likewise require some degree of green industrial protectionism.
Russia-Ukraine Crisis Watch: New OPEC+ production cuts raise oil prices and provide an economic boost to Russia (04.03.23) | Read here
Surprise additional OPEC+ oil production cuts will bolster Moscow’s ability to withstand sanctions in the short term and potentially test Western ability to enforce its price cap. Recent Western military equipment deliveries to Ukraine, including Polish MiG-29 fighter jets and German-designed Leopard tanks, continue to fuel speculation on timing of the expected Ukrainian counteroffensive; poor weather conditions in April are among the factors that suggest it is still some weeks away. Despite Russia’s arrest of US journalist Evan Gershkovich and a New START treaty data-sharing breakdown further raising tensions between Washington and Moscow, Eurasia Group’s scenarios and probabilities remain unchanged.
Asia
Japan: New carbon trading system begins in April, but implementation will be gradual (03.31.23) | Read here
Japan announced its carbon pricing scheme would go into effect this April, to be implemented in stages between 2023 and 2027. Since the carbon trading and pricing scheme will be implemented gradually, the short-term impact on emissions will be minimal. Impact on emissions by 2030 will depend on the pricing and enforcement measures, which are still under discussion. Japan's new carbon pricing system aligns with the timeline of the EU CBAM, which includes a tax period beginning in 2026, and represents another signal that the G7 members might be closer to formally aligning their climate policies.
North America
Critical Minerals: Geopolitical turbulence will push North America to deepen supply chain integration and pursue new battery chemistries (04.03.23) | Read here
The following report is the first in a series from Eurasia Group’s new Critical Minerals Working Group, a cross-disciplinary assemblage of analysts from the following practices: Energy, Climate & Resources; Industrials & Supply Chains, and Geo-technology. It also leverages the work of specialists from regional and global macro practices. In coordination with Eurasia Group’s inaugural US-Canada Summit, this first report will focus on the role of CMs in North America.
Middle East and Africa
UAE: Authorities will seek to marginally reduce Russian economic ties (04.05.23) | Read here
Given the risks that sanctions evasion could create, Emirati authorities will explore ways to reduce scrutiny of the country’s linkages with Russian entities. The UAE will likely seek to manage risks on the financial side and more carefully weigh the footprint of Russian financial institutions and companies in the economy; some curtailing of non-oil goods trade with Russia is also possible. However, any initiatives will remain modest and focused on risk/reputation management; significantly reducing the presence of Russian individuals or entities in the UAE is unlikely.
Saudi Arabia, Egypt: Sisi’s trip to Riyadh affirms strategic link and opens door to Arab normalization with Syria (04.03.23) | Read here
Egyptian President Abdelfattah el Sisi’s meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman on 2 April highlights the resilience of the strategic bond between the two countries. Saudi Arabia’s financial support to Egypt will require still more progress on reforms by Cairo that might prove challenging, but a withdrawal of assistance is unlikely. Riyadh is likely to normalize relations with Syria, and Sisi has received explicit support from Riyadh to also move toward normalization; Saudi Arabia’s regional initiatives are focused on easing regional tensions to improve its geopolitical influence and security environment.
Sector Research
Energy, Climate and Resources: Amid geopolitical and energy security concerns, technology breakthroughs will drive global green transition (04.03.23)
The energy transition is happening globally, but it will look different and progress at varying speeds in each country and region; geopolitical factors will play a role as will individual countries’ economic circumstances, domestic energy resources, and politics. Technology breakthroughs are enabling more rapid decarbonization, with power and road transport moving more quickly along this path, while new possibilities are emerging for long-haul transport and heavy manufacturing. Tensions between emerging and industrialized markets will continue to grow as financing for energy transitions in lower-income countries remains insufficient and the costs of climate impacts are rising rapidly.
